title: Promise-BPP derandomization implying EXP circuit hardness
formal: Does complete deterministic derandomization of bounded-error polynomial-time promise problems force a deterministic exponential-time language to require superpolynomial Boolean circuits? Precisely, is the implication \[\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\] true?
why: Determine whether full promise-problem derandomization necessarily yields deterministic exponential-time circuit hardness, closing a central gap between efficient algorithms and nonuniform lower bounds.
status_note: The 2012 primary question and the 2024 Heavy Avoid discussion support retaining this implication as source-open. A bounded literature check on 14 September 2026 did not locate its resolution. Known nondeterministic, uniform or additional-assumption results have different targets; their proofs were not independently verified.

sentences: Derandomization replaces efficient bounded-error randomized algorithms by deterministic ones.
The question assumes this replacement for promise problems and asks whether it forces an exponential-time language to lack polynomial-size Boolean circuits.
Known implications involving nondeterministic exponential time do not establish the deterministic-class target.
The issue is a converse to hardness-based pseudorandomness constructions.
The project seeks to explain whether eliminating randomness necessarily reveals an explicit source of circuit hardness at the corresponding deterministic computational scale.

definitions: All languages and promise inputs are binary strings. A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\); only inputs in \(Y\cup N\) require a correct answer. It is in \(\mathrm{prBPP}\) if a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine halts in \(C(n+1)^a\) steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random tape, for constants \(C,a\) depending on the machine, accepts every input in \(Y\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and accepts every input in \(N\) with probability at most \(1/3\). Random bits are independent and fair. The class \(\mathrm{prP}\) has the same total polynomial clock and promise requirement with a deterministic machine and exact correctness. The hypothesis quantifies over all promise pairs, with a potentially different deterministic machine and polynomial for each pair; it does not require a single effective transformation of programs. There is no correctness requirement off the promise. Define \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^a})\), with standard constant-factor time bounds, and \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\). A Boolean circuit has \(n\) input bits, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants, unrestricted fan-out and one output bit. Its size is its number of non-input gates, including constant gates. Let \(s_L(n)\) be the minimum circuit size computing the characteristic function of \(L\) on every length-\(n\) input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) when \(s_L(n)\le C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\); its circuits need not be generated uniformly. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language \(L\in\mathrm{EXP}\) such that, for every integers \(k\ge1\), \(C\ge1\) and \(N_0\ge1\), some \(n\ge N_0\) satisfies \(s_L(n)>C(n+1)^k\). Hardness at infinitely many lengths is sufficient; hardness at all sufficiently large lengths is not part of the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation, using these promise, uniformity and circuit-size definitions. A negative answer must establish \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) together with \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\); a relativized counterexample only proves a relativization limitation. A lower bound in a nondeterministic class, a different hard language for each polynomial exponent, or a theorem with an additional unproved hypothesis does not establish the requested implication.

context_blocks.text: A promise separates the inputs on which an algorithm must answer correctly from those on which either answer is acceptable. This permits randomized decision procedures whose acceptance probability is guaranteed to avoid an intermediate interval only on valid inputs. The hypothesis derandomizes every such promise problem, and is stronger than merely identifying the classes of total decision languages.

Uniform algorithms use one finite program at every input length. A nonuniform circuit family may contain unrelated circuits at different lengths. The conclusion says that some language with a deterministic exponential-time algorithm still defeats every polynomial size bound in this more permissive computational model.

Vadhan states the question as Open Problem 8.8 for E and notes its equivalence to the EXP formulation. The distinction matters in stronger exponential lower bounds, but it does not change the polynomial-circuit separation requested here.

The surrounding source discussion records a consequence for NEXP, the nondeterministic exponential-time class. It also records a consequence giving, for each fixed circuit exponent, a hard language in NP. Neither statement supplies the single deterministic exponential-time language required by this card.

Lu, Oliveira, Ren and Santhanam still describe the necessity of nonuniform circuit hardness for derandomization as an open issue in their 2024 paper. Their Heavy Avoid results include uniform and infinitely-often characterizations; these have distinct quantifiers and do not assert the present implication.

A positive answer would show that fully eliminating bounded-error randomness necessarily entails a circuit lower bound at a deterministic exponential-time scale. This is a necessity question about derandomization: proving that some particular hardness assumption suffices for derandomization answers a different direction.
